text: You're building a new application for Acme Corp: Visitor Management, which tracks visitors checking in at corporate offices, prints badges, and logs each visit. You've just finished the Studio wizard from Lesson 20 and created the application with Scope ID Visitor Management, scope identifier x_acme_vms, and version 1.0.0 — chosen deliberately, following the vendor-prefix naming convention, knowing it's permanent the moment the application is saved.

First, naming the tables. Visitor Management needs a Visitor table for profile information and a Visit Log table for check-in and check-out times, host employee, and badge number. Applying Lesson 19's convention, you name them Visitor and Visit Log in Studio, and ServiceNow produces the real names x_acme_vms_visitor and x_acme_vms_visit_log. A Business Rule on Visit Log never has to type that prefix explicitly — current is already scoped to the real table it's running on, so naming isolation works quietly in the background.

Next, a Script Include called BadgeNumberFormatter, which generates a formatted badge number string from a visitor record. Nothing outside Visitor Management has any legitimate reason to call this — it's purely internal formatting logic for this one application's own badges. You leave Accessible From at its default, This Application Scope Only. There's no legitimate outside caller, so widening access would be an unnecessary, unaudited grant for a Script Include nothing else should ever need.

Then, DirectoryLookup, which looks up an employee by badge ID or name to find the host a visitor is there to see. It turns out this same lookup logic is also genuinely needed by the core ITSM scope, x_acme_itsm, to resolve an employee's manager chain for unrelated ticket-routing logic. That's a real cross-scope need, so the badge utility's leave-it-closed answer doesn't apply here.

Because DirectoryLookup touches real employee data, not a harmless formatting utility, the better choice is a targeted Cross-Scope Access Control grant to x_acme_itsm specifically, rather than opening it to every scope on the instance. That keeps DirectoryLookup closed to the rest of the instance by default, while giving the one legitimate caller exactly the access it needs — auditable, least-privilege, and reversible if x_acme_itsm ever stops needing it.

Every piece built in this lab — both tables, both Script Includes, and the Cross-Scope Access Control record — is automatically filed under x_acme_vms in Studio's application explorer, exactly as Lesson 22 described. A naming convention that prevents collisions, a default that keeps access closed unless there's a real reason to open it, and a targeted grant when that reason exists, all organized into one coherent application. Next up: Chapter Six, designing a real custom application's data model.
